title: Component subroutine: BGH fixed-endpoint Ham-path theorem invoked but not proved / mis-stated

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
**Severity: critical (load-bearing).**

The entire polynomial-time claim for the strong-component subroutine — and therefore the main theorem — rests on Theorem 3 (the cited "Bang-Jensen–Gutin–Huang merging algorithm"), which is *invoked, not proved*. The solution explicitly says: "We invoke Theorem 3 as the only external ingredient of this paper." A load-bearing external theorem must be (a) stated precisely as in the literature, (b) its hypotheses verified, (c) its conclusion shown to give exactly what is needed — or proved in full.

**Statement mismatch with the literature.** The classical Bang-Jensen–Gutin–Huang results give polynomial algorithms for the *unrestricted* Hamiltonian path and the Hamiltonian cycle in path-mergeable digraphs. Theorem 3 as written claims a polynomial algorithm for the **fixed-endpoint** Hamiltonian $(s,t)$-path for arbitrary prescribed $s,t$. An unrestricted Hamiltonian-path algorithm does not immediately yield a fixed-endpoint algorithm.

**Lemma 3 does not bridge the gap.** Section 4.2's source/sink augmentation produces a digraph $D'$ with a *unique* source $\hat s$ and *unique* sink $\hat t$; "source-to-sink Hamiltonicity" on $D'$ is itself another *fixed-endpoint* instance. Hence Lemma 3 reduces fixed-endpoint to fixed-endpoint and does not reduce to the unrestricted Hamiltonian-path problem that the cited literature result actually solves. The needed primitive is still assumed.

**What must be done.** Either (i) cite the precise theorem from the literature that solves the fixed-endpoint case (statement + hypotheses verified), or (ii) better, exploit Lemma 3(2): a Hamiltonian $(s,t)$-path of $D[C]$ exists iff $D'$ has *any* Hamiltonian path (the in-degree-0 source and out-degree-0 sink pin the endpoints), thereby reducing $\mathrm{HP}(C;s,t)$ to the *unrestricted* Hamiltonian-path decision on the path-mergeable digraph $D'$ — the problem the classical algorithm actually solves. The write-up currently cites a fixed-endpoint theorem instead of making this reduction.

(Note: the global reduction / forward DP of Theorem 2 was verified correct empirically on ~3000 brute-force-certified path-mergeable digraphs with 0 mismatches; the gap is confined to the component subroutine.)
